newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Baker can't say yet if U.N. Sahara plan will work.
newsitem.headline: Baker can't say yet if U.N. Sahara plan will work.

text.p: U.N. envoy James Baker said on Monday he could not yet determine whether it would be possible to carry out a long-delayed U.N. peace plan for Western Sahara involving a referendum on the future of the former Spanish colony.

He was speaking to reporters after briefing the Security Council on talks he chaired in London over the week-end with representatives of Morocco, which seeks to incorporate the disputed territory, and of the Polisario Front, which is campaigning for its independence.
"I'm not yet in position to answer the secretary-general's question, 'Can the settlement plan be implemented, either with or without adjustments ?' It's too early to tell that," Baker said.

The former U.S. secretary of state was named Annan's special envoy for Western Sahara earlier this year to advise whether the U.N. plan that originally called for a referendum in January 1992 could still be implemented.
The referendum has been repeatedly delayed because of differences between the two sides over who should be eligible to vote.
Baker, who held an earlier round of talks in Lisbon last month, said the latest round resulted in "some things...that haven't happened before in this long-simmering and intractable dispute."

He listed these as direct face-to-face talks between the parties under U.N. auspices; a compromise agreement on questions relating to the identification of voters that had held up the process; a compromise agreement regarding refugee issues; and agreement on confinement of Moroccan forces during a referendum period.
The parties had agreed to meet again on Aug. 29 and 30, though the venue had not yet been decided, he said.
Difficult issues still to be resolved concerned a code of conduct governing a referendum, prisoners of war, political detainees and the confinement of Polisario forces during a referendum.
Baker praised the "very constructive and positive attitude on the part of both of these parties," who had departed in some respects from some of their traditional positions.
This showed that "they really do want to implement the settlement plan. But we will have to wait and see," he said, stressing that nothing would be decided until everything had been decided.

Asked to compare his U.N. role with his work as a senior U.S. officials, Baker said: "It is similar in some respects, but sometimes you might want -- not in this dispute, I'm quick to add -- but sometimes you might want to wish for the 101st airborne, but no often," he joked, referring to a U.S. paratroop division often activated in times of crisis.
